veejay.x: 1982, from pronunciation of V.J., from video, on model of deejay (see disk). "One who presents a programme of (popular music) videos, esp. on television" [OED, 1989].

veggie.x: slang shortening of vegetable (n.), 1976; earlier vegie (1955). Related: Veggies.

vendee.x: "person to whom something is sold," 1540s; see vend (v.) + -ee.

vender.x: 1590s, agent noun in native form from vend (v.). Compare vendor.

vendue.x: "public sale, auction," 1680s, from Dutch vendu, from obsolete French vendue "sale, selling price," from vendre "to sell," from Latin vendere (see vend).

verger.x: "one who carries a verge (staff or rod) as an officer of the church," c. 1400, probably from Anglo-French *verger, from verge (see verge (n.)). Especially one who carries a verge before a bishop or other ecclesiastical authority. Related: Vergeress.

vermi-.x: word-forming element of Latin origin, "of, pertaining to, full of, or resembling worms," from Latin vermis "a worm," from PIE *urmi- "snake, worm" (de Vaan), source also of English worm, and according to Watkins from root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend."

vervet.x: South African monkey, 1884, from French (Cuvier), of unknown origin, perhaps short for vert grivet, literally "a green grivet," indicating it was greener than the kind of monkey known as a grivet (itself a name of unknown origin). "Vervets are among the monkeys carried about by organ-grinders" [Century Dictionary, 1891].

vestal.x:
"chaste, pure, virgin, characteristic of a Vestal," 1590s, originally (early 15c.) "belonging to or dedicated to Vesta" (q.v.), Roman goddess of hearth and home, from Latin vestalis.
The noun is recorded from mid-15c., short for Vestal virgin (Latin virgines Vestales), one of four (later six) priestesses in charge of the sacred fire, supposedly carried by Aeneas from the wreck of Troy, in the temple of Vesta in Rome. From 1580s in reference to any virgin or chaste woman.
 They entered the service of the goddess at from six to ten years of age, their term of service lasting thirty years. They were then permitted to retire and to marry, but few did so, for, as vestals, they were treated with great honor, and had important public privileges. Their persons were inviolable, any offense against them being punished with death, and they were treated in all their relations with the highest distinction and reverence. A vestal who broke her vow of chastity was immured alive in an underground vault amid public mourning. There were very few such instances; in one of them, under Domitian, the chief of the vestals was put to death under a false charge trumped up by the emperor. [Century Dictionary]

vicuna.x: Peruvian ruminant related to the llama and alpaca, c. 1600, from Spanish vicuña, from Quechua (Inca) wikuna, the native name of the animal. Another 17c. form of the name was vigogne, vicogne, from the French form.

video-.x: 20c. word-forming element of Latin origin; see video (adj.).

vinous.x: early 15c., "consisting of or containing wine;" 1660s, "having the qualities or nature of wine;" from Latin vinosus "full of wine; fond of wine," from vinum "wine" (see wine (n.)). Vinolent "given to drinking" (late 14c.) is from Latin vinolentus "intoxicated, full of or drunk with wine."

violet.x:
small wild plant with purplish-blue flowers, c. 1300, from Old French violete (12c.), diminutive of viole "violet," from Latin viola "the violet, a violet color," cognate with Greek ion (see iodine), probably from a pre-Indo-European substrate Mediterranean language.
The color name (late 14c., violet-blu) developed from the flower; compare Latin violaceus "of a violet color," borrowed in English 1650s as violaceous. There is also a Middle English violate (adj.) "flavored with violets" (mid-15c.). Related: Violescent "tending to a violet color."

vizard.x: "mask," 1550s, altered form of vysar, viser (see visor), by influence of words in -ard. The figurative use is attested from 1570s; common 17c. Also applied to the person with the masks, and used as a verb meaning "to conceal." Related: Vizarded; vizarding.

voodoo.x:
1820, Vaudoo, defined as "certain occult practices and the idolatrous worship of an African deity," from Louisiana French voudou, from a West African language such Fon vodun "deity, god." It is attested in 18c. French as a dance performed by African slaves. The verb is attested from 1880.
The spelling vodun in reference to the religion was popularized in 1930s by M. J. Herskovits, in an effort to disassociate it from negative and superstitious connotations of voodoo.

Vandyke.x: "short, pointed beard," 1894, from the style shown on portraits by Flemish painter Anton Van Dyck (1599-1641); earlier a type of collar with a deep cut edge (1755) also from a style depicted in his paintings.

Vaughan.x: from Welsh fychan, mutation of bychan "small."

Venturi.x: type of tube, 1887, in reference to Italian physicist Giovanni Battista Venturi (1746-1822).

Vinland.x:
by 1755, the name supposedly given by Leif Eriksson to lands he explored in northeastern North America c. 1000; the name appears in Old Norse sagas by early 13c. It could mean either "vine-land" or "meadow-land," and either way was perhaps coined to encourage settlement (compare Greenland).
That others might have found the New World before Columbus was popular knowledge: Irving's "History of New York" (1809) lists Noah along with Phoenician, Carthaginian, Tyrean, Chinese, German, and Welsh candidates, along with "the Norwegians, in 1002, under Biorn."
Evidence in the old sagas of a Norse discovery of North America had been noticed from time to time by those who could read them. The notion was seriously debated early 19c. by von Humboldt and other European scholars before winning general acceptance by the 1830s. The case for the identification of Vinland with North America began to be laid out in English-language publications in 1840. Lowell wrote a poem about it ("Hakon's Lay," 1855). Thoreau knew of it ("Ktaadn," 1864). Physical evidence of the Norse presence was uncovered by the excavations at L'Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland in 1960.

Volapuk.x: artificial language invented 1879 by Johann Martin Schleyer (1831-1912) based on cut-down words from English, Latin, and German. The name, in Volapük, is literally "world-speech," based on English world and speak. Related: Volapükist.

Vulgate.x: Latin translation of the Bible, especially that completed in 405 by St. Jerome (c.340-420) and accepted as authorized by the Catholic Church, c. 1600, from Medieval Latin Vulgata, from Late Latin vulgata "common, general, ordinary, popular" (in vulgata editio "popular edition"), from Latin vulgata, fem. past participle of vulgare "make common or public, spread among the multitude," from vulgus "the common people" (see vulgar). So called because the translations made the book accessible to the common people of ancient Rome.

vagitus.x: crying of a newborn child, 1650s, from Latin vagitus "a crying, squalling," from vagire (see sough (v.)).

vaguely.x: "in an uncertain manner, without distinctness or definition," 1748, from vague + -ly (2).

varnish.x:
mid-14c., vernish, "solution of resinous matter forming a clear, limpid fluid" used as a protective or decorative coating on wood, from Old French vernis "varnish" (12c.), from Medieval Latin vernix "odorous resin," a word of uncertain origin.
Perhaps it is from Late Greek verenike, from Greek Berenike, name of an ancient city in Libya (modern Bengasi) credited with the first use of varnishes. The town is named for Berenike II, queen of Egypt (see Berenice).
The figurative sense of "specious gloss, pretense; artificial covering to give a fair appearance to some act or conduct" is recorded from 1560s.

late 14c.; see varnish (n.). Related: Varnished; varnishing. Century Dictionary defines varnishing day as "A day before the opening of a picture exhibition on which exhibitors have the privilege of retouching or varnishing their pictures after they have been placed on the walls." The custom is said to date to the early years of 19c.

varsity.x: 1825, "university," variant of earlier versity (1670s), shortened form of university. Compare varsal (1690s), short for universal (used by Swift, Scott); varmint from vermin; and Grose's "Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue" (1788) has vardy as slang for verdict. "Used in English universities, and affected to some extent in American colleges" [Century Dictionary].

vegetal.x: "pertaining to or relating to a plant or plants," c. 1400, from Medieval Latin *vegetalis, from Latin vegetare "enliven, animate" (see vegetable (adj.)). Related: Vegetality.

velvety.x: "resembling velvet, soft and smooth to the eye or touch," mid-15c., velveti, from velvet + -y (2). Related: Velvetiness.

veranda.x:
also verandah, "open portico on the exterior of a building," with a roof on pillars and railing, 1711, Anglo-Indian, from Hindi varanda, which probably is from Portuguese varanda, originally "long balcony or terrace," a word of uncertain origin.
Possibly a European word used in an Indian context and found there by the English, who were relative late-comers to India. In which case it might represent Spanish baranda "railing," and be ultimately from Vulgar Latin *barra "barrier, bar." French véranda is borrowed from English.
 That the word as used in England and in France was brought by the English from India need not be doubted. But either in the same sense, or in one closely analogous, it appears to have existed, quite independently, in Portuguese and Spanish; and the manner in which it occurs without explanation in the very earliest narrative of the adventure of the Portuguese in India ... seems almost to preclude the possibility of their having learned it in that country for the first time .... [Col. Henry Yule and A.C. Burnell, "Hobson-Jobson, A Glossary of Colloquial Anglo-Indian Words and Phrases," 1903]

verbify.x: "make into a verb," 1813; see verb + -ify. Related: Verbification. A verbal noun verbing is attested from 1757 as "using of verbs."

verdure.x: late 14c., "greenness, fresh green color," from Old French verdure "greenness, greenery, green fields, herbs," from verd, variant of vert "green" (12c.), from Latin viridis "green" (source of Spanish, Italian verde), related to virere "be green," virescere "turn green," viridare "be green," all of which are of uncertain etymology. De Vaan writes, "None of the adduced set of cognates (Lat. 'green', Baltic 'multiply, fruit', Gm. 'sprout, meadow') undoubtedly belong together." The meaning "green plants, vegetation" is attested from c. 1400.

vermian.x: "of the nature of a worm," also, in zoology, "of or pertaining to the Vermes," 1867, from Latin vermis "worm" (see vermi-).

vernant.x: mid-15c., "flourishing as in spring," also figurative, from Old French vernant "vernal," from Latin vernantem (nominative vernans), present participle of vernare "to flourish, appear like spring," from vernus "of spring" (see vernal).

vernier.x: device with a small movable scale for making precise measurements, 1766, from name of inventor, French mathematician Pierre Vernier (1580-1637), who described it in 1631.

versant.x: 1640s, "busy" (with something), "anxious" (about), from Latin versantem (nominative versans), present participle of versare, literally "to turn often," frequentative of vertere "to turn" (from PIE root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend"). The meaning "familiar, acquainted, conversant" with a subject or person is from 1787. There is an earlier use of it as "inclined to reverse a decision" (mid-15c.) from Latin versans.

vesicle.x: in anatomy, zoology, pathology, "small, bladder-like structure," early 15c., from French vesicule, from Latin vesicula (plural vesiculae) "little blister," diminutive of vesica "bladder, blister" (see vesica).

vetting.x: "treatment (of an animal) by a veterinarian," by 1899, verbal noun from vet (v.).

vilayet.x: "province of the Turkish empire," 1869, from Turkish, from Arabic wilayah "province," from wali "governor," from waliya "he reigned, governed."

voltaic.x: 1813, designating electricity produced by chemical action, formed in recognition of Italian physicist Alessandro Volta (1745-1827), who perfected a chemical process used in electrical batteries, + -ic.

vulture.x:
large type of Old Word raptor specially adapted for feeding mainly on carrion, late 14c., from Anglo-French vultur, Old French voutoir, voutre (Modern French vautour), from Latin vultur, earlier voltur, perhaps related to vellere "to pluck, to tear" (see svelte).
The name was applied to unrelated New World birds of similar features and habit. The figurative sense is recorded from 1580s, in reference to persons, "rapacity, thirst for prey." Related: Vulturine; vulturous.

Valencia.x: place in Spain, Roman Valentia Edetanorum "fort of the Edetani," a local people name; the first element from Latin valentia "strength" (see valence (n.)). Related: Valencian. Valenciens or valence were names given 14c. to kinds of cloth from or associated with Valencia, but the thin, fine fabrics also might be from Valenciennes, the town in northern France celebrated for lace manufacture.

Vaseline.x:
1872, trademark for an ointment made from petroleum and marketed by Chesebrough Manufacturing Co., coined from German Wasser "water" + Greek elaion "oil" + scientific-sounded ending -ine. The name preserves Robert A. Chesebrough's opinion that petroleum was a product of the underground decomposition of water.
 The name is of mixed origin, being derived from Wasser, water, and elaion [Greek in the original], oil (water-oil), and indicates the belief of the discoverer that petroleum, the mother of Vaseline, is produced by the agency of heat and pressure from the carbon of certain rocks, and the hydrogen of water. [The Monthly Review of Dental Surgery, February 1877]

Vauxhall.x: popular pleasure garden on south bank of Thames in London from c. 1661-1859; the name is Middle English Faukeshale (late 13c.), "Hall or manor of a man called Falkes," an Old French personal name.

Veronica.x:
fem. proper name, French Veronique, a variant of Greek Berenike (see Berenice). The popular "Saint Veronica" (not in the Roman Martyrology) traditionally was a pious woman who wiped the face of Christ when he fell carrying the cross to Calvary. The image of his face remained on the cloth, and the "veil of Veronica" has been preserved in Rome from the 8c.
Her popularity rose with the propagation of the Stations of the Cross, and this connection led to the folk-etymology derivation of the name from Latin vera "true" + Greek eikon "image." Some also identified her with the woman with the issue of blood, cured by Christ, as in the East this woman was identified from an early date by the name Berenike.
Hence vernicle (mid-14c.) "picture of the face of Christ," from Old French veronicle, variant of veronique "St. Veronica's cloth."

Vesuvius.x: volcano near Naples; the name is of unknown origin; perhaps from Celtic root *ves- "mountain" or Oscan fesf "smoke, steam." Related: Vesuvian. The great eruption that destroyed Pompeii began Aug. 24, 79 C.E.

Victrola.x: 1905, trademark of a phonograph, from Victor Talking Machine Co. According to a contemporary letter from company head Eldridge R. Johnson, coined because it had "a sound suggestive of music," with ending from pianola.

Vineland.x: city in southern New Jersey, 1861, said to have been named for the abundance of grapes; see vine (n.) + land (n.).

Voltaire.x: French dramatist, poet, and historian, name taken from 1718 by French author François Marie Arouet (1694-1778) after his imprisonment in the Bastille on suspicion of having written some satirical verses; originally de Voltaire. The signification is uncertain.

valerian.x: plant of Eurasia, cultivated for its medicinal root, c. 1300 (in Latin form in late Old English), from Old French valeriane "wild valerian" (13c.), apparently from feminine singular of Latin adjective Valerianus, from the personal name Valerius (see Valerie). Weekley writes, "some of the German and Scand. forms of the name point rather to connection with the saga-hero Wieland." Related: Valeric.

valorous.x: of persons or actions, "having or displaying valor; brave, courageous," late 15c. (Caxton), from French valeureux, from valeur (see valor). Related: Valorously; valorousness.

varicose.x: early 15c., varicous (Chauliac), "of or related to varix; characterized by swollen blood vessels," from Latin varicosus "with dilated veins," from varix (genitive varicis) "dilated vein," from varus "bent outward, bow-legged," which is of uncertain origin (see vary). Latin varix yielded Middle English varice "swollen blood vessel in the leg" (late 14c.).

varietal.x: 1849, "having the characteristics of a variety, of the nature of a subspecies," 1849, a biologists' word, from variety + -al (1). In reference to wines, "made from a single variety of grape," is attested by 1941, American English. As a noun, in this sense, attested from 1955. Related: Varietally.

variform.x: "varied in form, having different shapes," 1660s, from Latin varius (see vary) + forma "form, shape" (see form (n.)).

venation.x: "arrangement of veins or vessels" in botany of plant structures, in entomology of insect wings, 1640s, of plants, noun of state from Latin vena "vein" (see vein). Related: Venational.

vengeful.x: "disposed to take revenge, vindictive, cruel, malevolent, characterized by vengeance," 1580s, from obsolete venge (v.) "take revenge" + -ful. Earlier adjectives in similar senses include vengeable (late 14c.), vengaunt (mid-14c.), vengerous. An adverb vengancely is attested from mid-15c. Related: Vengefully; vengefulness.

vermouth.x: alcoholic cordial, white wine flavored with aromatic herbs, 1806, vermuth, from French vermouth (18c.), from German Wermuth "wormwood," from Middle High German wermuot, from Old High German wermuota (see wormwood), name of the aromatic herb formerly used in the flavoring of the liqueur.

vesicant.x:
"a blistering agent," 1660s, from Medieval Latin vesicantem (nominative vesicans), present participle of vesicare, from vesica "a bladder, a blister," hence "a bag, a purse, etc." (see vesica).
From 1826 in modern use as an adjective, "producing a blister, causing blisters" (Chauliac, early 15c. also has it in this sense).

vespillo.x: also vespillone, "he that carries forth dead bodies in the night to be buried, as they use in time of plague and great sickness" [Blount], 1630s, now obsolete, from Latin vespillonis "one who carried out the bodies of the dead poor at night," from vesper "evening" (see vesper).

vestment.x: c. 1200, "liturgical garment worn by clergy during divine services," from Old French vestment (12c., Modern French vêtement), from Latin vestimentum "clothing, clothes," from vestire "to clothe" (from PIE *wes- (4) "to clothe;" see wear (v.)). Related: Vestments; vestmental.

viburnum.x: genus of shrubs widespread in Eurasia and North America, the wayfaring-tree, 1731, from Latin viburnum, which is said to be probably an Etruscan word.

vicarage.x: early 15c., "benefice of a vicar;" mid-15c., "house or residence of a vicar;" from vicar + -age.

villainy.x: c. 1200, vileinie, "extreme depravity, foul or infamous wrongdoing, shameful condition, atrocious wickedness," from Anglo-French vilanie, Old French vilenie "low character, unworthy act, disgrace, degradation," from vilain (see villain). By c. 1300 as "churlishness, rudeness; discourteous or abusive language."

vinculum.x: plural vincula, "a bond, tie," 1670s, from Latin vinculum "that with which anything is bound," from stem of vincire "to bind" (see *weik- (2)). In mathematics, in reference to the line drawn above terms subject to the same operation, by 1710.

viridian.x:
shade of green, 1882, from the paint color name (1862), coined from Latin virid-, stem of viridis "green, blooming, vigorous" (see verdure) + -ian.
English earlier had viridity (early 15c.) "greenery, greenishness, verdure;" virid (adj.) "green, blooming" (c. 1600). Viridescent "greenish" is attested from 1788 in mineralogy; viridescence (n.) by 1830 in botany.

visitant.x: 1650s, "visiting, acting the part of a visitor," from French visitant, present-participle of visiter (see visit (v.)). As a noun, "one who visits," 1590s; in reference to migratory birds that stay all or part of a season, 1770.

vitalize.x: 1670s, "give an organic character to," from vital + -ize. The figurative sense of "animate, make active" is attested by 1805. Related: Vitalized; vitalizing.

voidable.x: "capable of being voided" in any sense, late 15c., from void (v.) + -able.

Valentino.x: "gigolo, good-looking romantic man," 1927, from Italian-born U.S. movie actor Rudolph Valentino (1895-1926), who was adored by female fans. His full name was Rodolfo Guglielmi di Valentino, from the Latin masc. proper name Valentinus (see Valentine).

Vicksburg.x: city in Mississippi, U.S., incorporated 1825, named for an early settler the Rev. Newitt Vick, who was said to have come to the region c. 1812 from Virginia with his family and chosen the town site in 1819. The Civil War siege lasted from May 23 to July 4, 1863.

Villanova.x: European culture of the early Iron Age, 1901, named for a hamlet near Bologna where archaeological remains of it were found. Related: Villanovan.

Virgilian.x: "of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the great Roman epic poet Virgil" (Publius Vergilius Maro, 70-19 B.C.E.), 1510s, from Latin Virgilianus. Also in Virgilian lots (Latin sortes Virgilianae), opening Virgil at random as an oracle.

Vulpecula.x: constellation added to the celestial map in 1687 by Johannes Hevelius, from Latin vulpecula, volpecula "little fox," diminutive of vulpes, volpes "fox" (see vulpine). A tiny dim constellation (only one star of it reaches 4th magnitude), in full Vulpecula cum Anserae, the fox with the goose, there were attempts to make a separate figure of the goose.

vaginitis.x: "inflammation of the vagina," 1833, medical Latin; see vagina + -itis "inflammation."

vainglory.x: c. 1200, vein-glorie, "worthless glory, meaningless honor, undue pomp or show," waynglori, from Old French vaine glorie, from Medieval Latin vana gloria "empty glory" (see vain + glory (n.)).

vampirism.x: "belief in the existence of vampires; act or practice of blood-sucking;" 1737; see vampire + -ism.

vandalize.x: by 1797, a back-formation from vandalism or else from vandal + -ize. Related: Vandalized; vandalizing; vandalization. A past participle vandald is recorded from 1640s.

vaporetto.x: Venetian public transit canal-motorboat, 1926, from Italian vaporetto, diminutive of vapore "steam," from Latin vapor (see vapor (n.)).

vaporizer.x: "one who or that which converts to vapor; atomizer," 1846, agent noun from vaporize. A vaporer (1650s) was one who swaggers or bullies (see vapors).

varicella.x: specific contagious disease of childhood, "chicken-pox," medical Latin, 1764, irregular diminutive of variola (see variola). Related: Varicellous.

vasectomy.x: operation to render a male infertile, 1896, from Modern Latin vas (deferens) + -ectomy "a cutting, surgical removal." Related: Vasectomized.

vassalage.x: c. 1300, from Old French vassalage, vasselage "the service of a vassal," from vassal (see vassal).

velveteen.x: imitation velvet (with cotton in place of silk), 1776, velvetean, from velvet + commercial suffix -een (variant of -ine). An earlier imitation product was velveret (1769).

ventricle.x: late 14c., "small chamber or cavity within a bodily organ," especially of the heart, from Latin ventriculus (in reference to the heart, ventriculus cordis), literally "little belly," diminutive of venter (genitive ventris) "belly" (see ventral). Related: Ventricular.

venturous.x: "daring, fearless, intrepid, bold, hardy; involving hazard or risk," 1560s, a shortened form of adventurous, influenced by venture.

verbarian.x:
"word-coiner," 1873, from Latin verbum "word" (see verb) + -arian. Fitzedward Hall ("Modern English"), coined it in a footnote, describing Southey, comparing him in this quality to Rabelais, Thomas Nashe, Taylor the Water-poet, and 17c. Puritan commentator Owen Feltham. Hall would know one. Compare verbiculture.
Coleridge (or the unnamed friend he was paraphrasing in a footnote) had used it earlier as an adjective, and with a different sense, in wishing for: "a verbarian Attorney-General, authorised to bring informations ex officio against the writer or editor of any work in extensive circulation, who, after due notice issued, should persevere in misusing a word" ("Church and State," 1830).

verbosity.x: "use of more words than necessary by a speaker or writer; state or character of being verbose," 1540s, from French verbosité (16c.) or directly from Late Latin verbositas, from Latin verbosus "full of words" (see verbose).

verdurous.x: "covered with vegetation or with a fresh green color," c. 1600, from verdure + -ous.

veritable.x:
early 15c., "upright, honest;" mid-15c., "agreeable to truth, grounded in reality," from Anglo-French and Old French veritable "true, real, truthful, valid (in law)," from verité (see verity) + -able.
Probably lost mid-17c. and reborrowed or revived after 1830 in emphatic use, "the very," hence extended use, by 1862, to denote "having all the distinctive qualities of." Related: Veritably.

vermifuge.x: 1690s, "remedy to expel intestinal worms," from French vermifuge, from Latin vermis "worm" (from PIE root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend") + fugare "cause to flee, put to flight" (see fugitive (adj.)).

vermilion.x: late 13c., vermiloun, "cinnabar, naturally occurring mercuric sulfide; red dye made from ground cinnabar," from Anglo-French and Old French vermeillon "red lead, cinnabar, (cosmetic) rouge" (12c.), from vermeil (see vermeil). As an adjective, "of the color of vermilion," by 1580s.

verminous.x: 1610s, "of or like vermin;" 1630s, "infested with vermin, foul or offensive on account of parasitic vermin," from vermin + -ous or else from Latin verminosus.

verrucous.x: "warty, full of warts," 1650s, from Latin verrucosus "full of warts," from verruca "wart" (see verruca). Related: Verrucose (1680s).

vertebral.x: 1680s, "pertaining or relating to vertebrae;" see vertebra + -al (1). By 1847 as "of the nature of a vertebrae." Of animals, "having a backbone," by 1816. Vertebrate (adj.) in this sense is by 1826.

vesicular.x: in anatomy and zoology, "pertaining to a vesicle; having vesicles," 1715, from Modern Latin vesicularis, from vesicula "little blister," diminutive of vesica "bladder, blister" (see vesica). Related: Vesiculation; vesiculated (1703); vesiculous (1690s).

vestibule.x:
1620s, "a porch of a door," later "antechamber, lobby" (1730), from French vestible, from Latin vestibulum "enclosed fore-court between a house and the street;" by extension, " an entrance, a beginning;" a word of unknown origin. According to de Vaan, "Many different etymologies have been proposed," but "all of them are semantically unsatisfactory."
It is attested from mid-15c. in the obsolete variant form vestible "roofless, enclosed area." In anatomy, in reference to the ear part, from 1728.

vestigial.x: 1850, "of, pertaining to, or of the nature of a vestige; like a mere trace of what has been," originally in biology, from vestige + -al (1).

viability.x: "capability of living," especially immediately after removal from the womb, 1823, from French viabilité, from viable (see viable). In natural history, the ability to live in certain conditions (1883).

victimize.x: also victimise, "make a victim of," 1826 (implied in victimizing), from victim + -ize. Colloquial sense of "cheat, swindle" is by 1839. Related: Victimized; victimizable (1842); victimizer (1831). An earlier verb was victimate "kill as a sacrifice" (1610s).

videotape.x: 1953, "magnetic tape for video recordings," from video + tape (n.). By 1960 as "a video recording." The verb is by 1958, from the noun. Related: Videotaped; videotaping.

vindemial.x:
"belonging to a vintage or grape harvest," 1650s, from Late Latin vindemialis, from Latin vindemia "a gathering of grapes, yield of grapes," from combining form of vinum "wine" (see wine (n.)) + stem of demere "take off" (from de- "from, away from" + emere "to take;" from PIE root *em- "to take, distribute").
Related: Vindemiate (v.); vindemiation (c. 1600). Also Vindemiatrix, the name given in the Alfonsine Tables to an unremarkable star in the constellation Virgo (the name is attested in English by 1704), a feminization of the name given to it by Latin authors, vindemiator, vindemitor, literally "grape-gatherer, vintager." Evidently its heliacal rising or setting at some ancient era coincided importantly with the Italian vintage.

virginity.x:
c. 1300, virginite, "chastity, state of being a virgin, state or quality of being a young woman without sexual experience," considered the natural state of an unmarried woman, from Anglo-French and Old French virginite "(state of) virginity; innocence" (10c. in Old French), from Latin virginitatem (nominative virginitas) "maidenhood, virginity," from virgo (see virgin).
By early 14c. it is attested as "condition of voluntarily remaining physically chaste, deliberate abstinence from sexual relations," sometimes extended to freedom from sexual thoughts. Related: Virginhood (1660s).

vis-a-vis.x: "in a position facing one another," 1755, from French prepositional use of the adj. vis-à-vis "face to face," from vis "face" (see visage). It also was used 18c. of vehicles with seats arranged so occupants face one another.

visualise.x: chiefly British English spelling of visualize. For suffix, see -ize. Related: Visualised; visualising; visualisation.

vitelline.x: "colored like an egg yolk," early 15c., from Latin vitellus. In biology, of the substance of an egg yolk, by 1835.

vitiation.x: "impairment, corruption," 1630s, from Latin vitiationem (nominative vitiatio) "violation, corruption," noun of action from past-participle stem of vitiare "to make faulty, injure, spoil, corrupt," from vitium "fault, defect, blemish, crime, vice" (see vice (n.1)).

voiceless.x: 1530s, "unable to speak, mute, dumb," from voice (n.) + -less. The meaning "having no say in affairs" is from 1630s; that of "unspoken, unuttered" is from 1816. In phonology, "unvoiced," from 1867. Related: Voicelessly; voicelessness.

volcanism.x:
"phenomena connected with volcanoes; state or character of being volcanic;" 1819, from French volcanisme, from volcan (see volcano). Related: Volcanity (1796). Alternative vulcanism is attested by 1877.
 The words volcano and volcanic are firmly fixed in English, and the former is in universal and exclusive use among those who speak that language. Hence all the derivatives should be spelled correspondingly ; thus, volcanism, volcanicity, volcanology, and not vulcanism etc. [Century Dictionary, 1891]

voyeurism.x: "scopophilia, state or condition of being a voyeur," 1913; see voyeur + -ism. Related: Voyeurist (1955), a needless variant.

vulgarian.x: "vulgar person," especially "rich person of low ideas and vulgar tastes and manners," 1804, from vulgar (adj.) + -ian.

vulgarise.x: chiefly British English spelling of vulgarize (q.v.); for suffix, see -ize. Related: Vulgarised; vulgarising; vulgarisation.

vulgarism.x: 1640s, "phrase or expression used in common speech" (a sense now obsolete); see vulgar (adj.) + -ism. By 1748 as "a low colloquialism."

vulgarity.x:
1570s, "the common people," from French vulgarité and directly from Late Latin vulgaritas "the multitude," from vulgaris (see vulgar). The meaning "coarseness, crudeness, want of refinement; a vulgar act or expression" is recorded from 1774.
There is a vulgarious in Middle English as "vernacular," of language.
 Out of Franssh now it is translated into oure reude volgaries moders tonge. ["The Secret of Secrets," c. 1450]

vulgarize.x: "make common or popular" (transitive), by 1709, from vulgar (adj.) + -ize. By 1756 as "debase, degrade." From c. 1600 in an intransitive sense of "act in a vulgar way." Related: Vulgarized; vulgarizing.

vulnerary.x: "useful in healing wounds," 1590s, from Latin vulnerarius "of or pertaining to wounds," from vulnus "a wound" (see vulnerable).

vulpicide.x: "one who kills a fox" other than by hunting with hounds, 1826, from Latin vulpes "fox" (see vulpine) + -cide. By 1873 as "the killing of a fox."

Vanderbilt.x: generic name for "millionaire, excessively rich person," by 1885, American English, in reference to Cornelius Vanderbilt, U.S. railroad and shipping magnate (1794-1877) and his heirs.

vaginismus.x: "spasmodic narrowing of the orifice of the vagina," 1861, medical Latin, from vagina + -ismus (see -ism).

varicocele.x: type of tumor in the scrotum, 1736, medical Latin, from Latin varico-, combining form of varix "dilated vein," (see varicose) + Latinized form of Greek kele "tumor, rupture, hernia" (see -cele).

vaticinate.x:
"to prophecy, foretell," 1620s, a back formation from vaticination or else from Latin vaticinatus, past participle of vaticinari "foretell, predict," from vates (see vates) + formative element -cinus. Related: Vaticinated; vaticinating; vaticinal; vaticinator; vaticinatress.
 The verb, formerly equivalent to prophesy, now usually connotes contempt & means rather to play the prophet, to be a Cassandra ; vaticination is similarly limited. [Fowler, "Modern English Usage," 1926]

vegetative.x:
late 14c., vegetatif, "endowed with the power of physical growth," especially of plants, from Old French vegetatif "(naturally) growing" and directly from Medieval Latin vegetativus, from vegetat-, past participle stem of vegetare (see vegetable (adj.)).
The Middle English transferred sense was "producing, promoting, or characterized by growth, animating, vivifying." In medieval philosophy and theology also "pertaining to the lowest level of soul, which gives bodily life, drives reproduction, etc." (early 15c.). Later the word was used in reference to animals, noting functions, processes, and other vital phenomena that act unconsciously or involuntarily (healing, digestion, reproduction) and are common to plants and animals, as distinguished from sensation, volition, etc. that seem exclusive to animals.
Hence the modern pathological sense of "brain-dead, lacking intellectual activity, mentally inert" (1893), via the notion of having only such functions common also to vegetable growth. Cockeram's "English Dictionarie" (1623) has Vegetive "Which liveth as plants do."

ventilator.x: "one who or that which ventilates," 1743, agent noun from ventilate. Medical device sense of "respirator" is by 1961. Latin ventilator meant "a winnower." Related: Ventilatory.

vertebrate.x: "a vertebrate animal," 1826, from Latin vertebratus "jointed, articulated" (Pliny), from vertebra "joint or articulation of the body, joint of the spine" (see vertebra). As an adjective also from 1826.

vespertine.x: mid-15c., "of the evening; belonging to or occurring in the evening," from Latin vespertinus "of the evening," from vesper "evening" (see vesper). Evening dew in old science could be humor vespertine. Of animals, "flying or otherwise active in evening," from c. 1600.

vestibular.x: "of or resembling a vestibule," 1819, in reference to the inner ear part, from vestibule + -ar.

viatecture.x:
"civil engineering," 1841, proposed ["Irreg." - OED 1989] by Roswell Park in "Pantology;" see via + architecture.
 WE propose the term Viatecture, as nearly synonymous with Civil Engineering, to include the construction of roads and bridges, railroads, and canals, and water works; and the improvement of rivers and harbors. [Park]
He wrote that civil engineering was an 18c. term meant to distinguish the work from military, but the word in either case applied to machines, and he proposed viatecture "to include a more limited and distinct range of objects all of which properly be comprehended as arts of conveyance."

vibraphone.x: musical instrument like a xylophone but with metal bars in place of wood, 1926, a Latin-Greek hybrid; see vibrato + -phone. So called for the vibrato that gives it its characteristic sound. Related: Vibraphonist.

victorious.x: "having overcome an antagonist or enemy; consistently triumphing over foes in battles, contests, etc.," late 14c., from Anglo-French victorious, Old French victorios, and directly from Late Latin victoriosus "having many victories," from victoria "victory" (see victory). Related: Victoriously; victoriousness.

villainous.x: c. 1300, "offensive, abusive, befitting a villain;" c. 1400, "despicable, shameful, morally corrupt;" from Old French vileneus "worthless, base," from vilain (see villain). Related: Villainously; villainousness; villainly (early 14c.).

vinaigrous.x: "sour like vinegar," 1837 (Carlyle), from vinegar (French vinaigre) + -ous. Originally and usually figurative, "crabby, cantankerous."

vindicator.x: "one who justifies, maintains, or defends," 1560s, from Late Latin vindicator "an avenger," from Latin vindicare (see vindication). Englished fem. form vindicatress is attested by 1854.

virtuality.x: late 15c., "possession of force," a sense now obsolete; 1640s as "essential being apart from external form;" see virtual + -ity. By 1836 as "a potentiality." Hence "state or quality of not being real."

vitrescent.x: "turning to glass, tending to become like glass," 1756, from Latin vitrum "glass" (see vitreous) + -escent. It might have been a poets' good word had the manufacturers not got to it first, along with vitrescence (1796) and less-poetic vitrescible (1754), vitrefacture (1842).

volatility.x: 1620s, "readiness to vaporize or evaporate;" see volatile (adj.) + -ity. By 1650s as "frivolous or giddy behavior." Rarely as "character of having the power of flight" (1822).

volumetric.x: in chemistry and physics, "pertaining to measure by volume," 1854, from volumeter "instrument for measuring the volume of liquids and gases" (1827) + -ic. Related: Volumetrical (1853); volumetrically.

vomitorium.x:
1754, "passage or opening in an ancient amphitheater leading to or from the seats," from Latin (Macrobius, Sat., VI.iv), from vomitare (see vomit (n.)) + -orium (see -ory). Also Englished as vomitory.
 The outside of the [Colosseum] was encrusted with marble, and decorated with statues. The slopes of the vast concave, which formed the inside, were filled and surrounded with sixty or eighty rows of seats of marble likewise, covered with cushions, and capable of receiving with ease about fourscore thousand spectators. Sixty-four vomitories (for by that name the doors were very aptly distinguished) poured forth the immense multitude; and the entrances, passages, and staircases were contrived with such exquisite skill, that each person, whether of the senatorial, the equestrian, or the plebeian order, arrived at his destined place without trouble or confusion. [Edward Gibbon, History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 1836.]
The meaning "place where ancient Romans (allegedly) deliberately vomited during feasts" is attested by 1869.

vasculature.x: "arrangement of the vascular system of the body," 1934, from Latin vascularis "of or pertaining to vessels or tubes" (see vascular) on model of musculature.

vasopressin.x: type of hormone, 1928, from vasopressor "causing the constriction of blood vessels" (see vaso-) + -in (2).

vellication.x: "action of pulling or twitching," 1620s, from Latin vellicationem (nominative vellicatio) "a plucking," also "a taunting," noun of action from past-participle stem of vellicare "to pinch, peck, pluck, nip," a derivative of vellere "to pull out, deprive of hair, feathers, etc." (see svelte).

vermiculite.x:
micaceous mineral, 1814, from Latin vermiculari (from vermiculus, diminutive of vermis "worm;" see vermi-) + -ite.
 When heated nearly to redness they exfoliate largely, and some kinds project out with a vermicular motion, as if they were a mass of small worms (whence the name). [Century Dictionary]

vichyssoise.x: 1925, as Creme Vichyssoise, from French crême vichyssoise, literally "Vichy style cream." A kind of potato-leek soup now known as a cold dish, in early references it could also be served hot. First appears on the menu of the old Ritz-Carlton in New York. Perhaps the connection is to the refreshing properties of Vichy water (see Vichy).

vinaigrette.x: 1690s, a type of condiment prepared with vinegar, from French vinaigrette (14c.), diminutive of vinaigre "(aromatic) vinegar" (see vinegar). Modern use in reference to a type of dressing for salads or cold vegetables is by 1877. Also, from 1811, "small bottle or box for carrying aromatic vinegar."

viniculture.x: "cultivation of (grape) vines," 1871, from combining form of Latin vinea "vine" (see vine). For second element, see culture (n.).

violoncello.x: modern form of the medieval viola da gamba, 1724, from Italian violoncello, diminutive of violone "bass viol," from viola (see viola) + augmentative suffix -one (see -oon). Related: Violoncellist.

voluntarism.x:
1838, "theory or principal of using voluntary action rather than coercion" (in politics, religion, etc.), from voluntary + -ism.
In philosophy, "theory that the will is the basic principle," 1896, from German Voluntarismus. As a synonym of volunteerism, denoting the involvement of volunteer organizations in social welfare, by 1957.
Voluntaryism in a religious sense, as opposed to establishmentarianism, is recorded from 1835 in the debate in England over interdependence of Church and state. It is attested by 1883 in reference to any system (of labor, etc.) based on voluntary principles or action.

Victorianism.x: 1865, in architecture, "building that is an example of Victorian style;" by 1872 in reference to a contemporary style in England, variously or vaguely described; from Victorian + -ism. In non-architectural use by 1902.

valorization.x: "act or fact of fixing the price of," 1906, from valor in its otherwise archaic sensed of "value, amount of money a thing is worth" (late 15c.).

vaporization.x: also vaporisation, "action or process of converting into vapor," 1788, noun of action from vaporize. In same sense Middle English had vaporacioun (late 14c.).

vaticination.x: c. 1600, "inspired or oracular prediction;" 1620s, "act or fact of uttering predictions and prophecies;" from Latin vaticinationem (nominative vaticinatio), noun of action from past-participle stem of vaticinari (see vaticinate).

vaudevillian.x: "performer in vaudeville shows," 1900, from vaudeville + -ian. A writer of theatrical vaudevilles was a vaudevillist (1839).

vegetability.x: "vegetable quality, character, or nature," 1640s; see vegetable (adj.) + -ity.

verbiculture.x: "the production of words," 1873, from Latin verbum "word" (see verb) + ending from agriculture, etc. Coined in "Modern English" by Fitzedward Hall, who was scolded for it in "Edinburgh Review" [July 1874] as an example of "far-fetched and scholastic phraseology." Verbicultural is attested from 1826.

veterinarian.x:
"animal doctor, one who practices the art of treating disease and injuries in domestic animals," 1640s, from Latin veterinarius "of or having to do with beasts of burden," also, as a noun, "cattle doctor," from veterinum "beast of burden;" veterinus "draft animals."
This is from vetus (genitive veteris) "old" (see veteran), possibly from the notion of "experienced," or of "one year old" (hence strong enough to draw burdens). The sense connection between "old" and "large domestic animal" is uncertain. De Vaan notes a theory that, as Latin veterinus usually referred to equines, horses had come to be seen "as 'the old stock' because by nature they lived longest of all cattle, and because the Romans did not as a rule eat horse meat."
Replaced native dog-leech (1520s).

vilification.x: "the act of defaming," 1650s, from Medieval Latin vilificationem (nominative vilificatio), noun of action from past-participle stem of Late Latin vilificare "make of little value" (see vilify). Donne (1620s) used it in a sense of "degradation, humiliation."

vociferation.x: "noisy exclamation, the act of clamoring," c. 1400, from Latin vociferationem (nominative vociferatio), "a loud calling, clamor, outcry," noun of action from past-participle stem of vociferari "to shout, yell, cry out" (see vociferate).
